title: Markov theory
content_html:
Markov theory

At its core, Markov theory is about how the future depends on the past. A system is Markovian if its next state depends only on its current state, not on the whole history of how it got there. This is called the Markov property. If you know the present perfectly, you don’t need the past - the present already contains everything relevant for predicting the future. The present is the summary of the past. That’s the Markov principle - it’s both a mathematical simplification and, intriguingly, a fair approximation of how many natural systems behave.

A Markov chain describes a system that hops between states with certain probabilities.

Current State Next State Probabilities
Sunny 0.8 → Sunny, 0.2 → Rain
Rain 0.4 → Sunny, 0.6 → Rain

From these transition probabilities, you can model how likely future states are, simulate random walks, or calculate equilibrium distributions. Markov models are everywhere:

  • Speech recognition and language models (early n-gram models)
  • Genetics (sequence patterns)
  • Reinforcement learning and control theory
  • Predictive processing models of the brain

Now, here’s the twist: a pure Markov system has no long-term memory - the past only matters insofar as it shapes the present state. But most real systems are not strictly Markovian. They have hidden variables that carry information from the past - even if you can’t see them directly. In such cases, the Markov property still holds in an expanded space:

If you include the hidden states, the full system is Markovian - but your partial view (the observations) seems to have “memory”.

In a Hidden Markov Model, there are hiidden states that evolve with Markov transitions, and observable signals that depend on those states. You can’t see the hidden state directly - so you infer it from the sequence of observations. That inference process - tracking what you believe about the hidden state - is a form of memory. The system itself is Markovian, but the observer must remember past evidence to estimate the hidden state. That’s exactly what the brain does.

Friston’s Free Energy Principle and the idea of a Markov blanket extend this to life and cognition. A Markov blanket defines the boundary between a system and its environment:

  • Internal states (the organism’s inner variables),
  • External states (the world),
  • Blanket states (sensory inputs and active outputs) that mediate between the two.

The blanket acts like the “interface” in a Markov system: Internal and external states don’t interact directly, only through sensory and motor channels. This makes the organism’s internal model conditionally independent of the world - given the blanket. Inside the blanket, the system must maintain beliefs about hidden external causes. It uses memory to infer what the world probably is and how it’s changing. So the external world evolves Markovianly (physics cares only about present states), but the internal system (the brain) must store a probabilistic model of hidden causes that are not directly accessible now - which requires memory. In other words, memory exists because, from within the Markov boundary, we can’t see all the variables - we must infer them from history.

Markov models in neuroscience

Concept Description Brain Analogy
State A configuration at time t Neural population activity pattern
Transition probability Likelihood of one state leading to another Synaptic dynamics, connectivity patterns
Hidden state Unobserved cause of sensory data External world or latent concept
Observation Sensory input Current perception
Belief update Infer hidden state from observations Memory and perception working together

The hippocampus, for instance, encodes state transitions in space and time (place cells, grid cells). When it replays experiences during sleep, it’s effectively sampling from a Markov model of the environment - consolidating transitions and sequences. From a physical perspective, each memory trace is a state attractor - a configuration that recurs because it is stable under the system’s dynamics. The brain drifts toward these attractors as it relaxes its prediction errors. So memory is the residue of past Markov transitions that the system reuses as priors for future inference.

In a deep sense, the Markov property is the minimal requirement for causal continuity: the idea that the universe progresses step by step, each state determining the next. Memory then represents the internalisation of that causal chain: matter evolves by local interactions (Markovian), life and mind emerge as systems that remember the hidden regularities so that they can anticipate the next transition more effectively.

Summary

Level Markov View Role of Memory
Physics Next state from current (no “memory”) None needed - full state observable
Chemistry / Biology Partial observability through boundaries Implicit memory in molecular feedback
Neural System Hidden external causes inferred Explicit memory of past evidence
Conscious Mind Model of its own Markov blanket Narrative memory; counterfactual inference

The world is (mostly) Markovian. Life is what happens inside a Markov blanket. Memory is what’s needed when you can’t see the full Markov state. It’s not that Markov theory creates memory - it shows why memory must exist for any observer that only ever sees part of the system.
